transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-08
Time: 15:00 - 16:02 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Priya Menon (Redwood AE), Luca Moretti (Redwood SE), Rosa Martinez (Acme Platform Eng), Ethan Cole (Acme ML Infra), Nadia Farouk (Acme CTO)

Auto-generated summary (may be noisy):
- Customer sees intermittent soft OOMs and occasional GPU watchdog timeouts under p95 traffic; happens more during longer sequences and some batched traffic patterns.
- SE suspects a combination of KV cache prefetch spikes, fragmentation from repeated model loads, and an older NVIDIA driver with a watchdog that's aggressive on the nodes.
- Immediate ask: gather nvprof/nvtrace, kernel logs (dmesg), nvidia-smi snapshots, and Redwood runtime traces.
- Next: repro session and Dedicated capacity pricing + security docs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Priya: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time, uh quick roll call, and then Luca will jump into the traces you sent, ok?
[00:08] Rosa: hi yep i'm here, rosa. ethan and nadia are on.
[00:11] Ethan: hey, morning, afternoon, thanks.
[00:13] Nadia: hi all.
[00:15] Luca: cool thanks, so i looked at the logs you pasted in the playbook, there's a few things that stand out. a lot of the failures are soft oom-like where the containerOOM event doesn't always show up but the process gets cuda-error-allocation, or a kernel launch timeout, and then we see watchdog reset messages in dmesg.
[00:32] Rosa: yeah that's what we see in prod, mostly at night when the batcher runs longer sequences — queries that are 3k+ tokens and we do 8-way batching. sometimes it just recovers, sometimes pods restart.
[00:46] Priya: can you clarify the batch size and the sequence lengths? you said 8-way batching, and 3k tokens — what's the quantized model run? int8? fp16?
[00:55] Ethan: we're running a 7B variant, q4_0 for most inference, but we flip to fp16 for specific routes. the model is loaded on GPU and we keep kv cache across requests.
[01:06] Luca: q4_0 is fine generally but mixing quant modes and hot-swapping can increase transient memory pressure. also kv-prefetch spikes can allocate temp buffers.
[01:14] Rosa: hmm ok so could the prefetch be the thing? we do a prefix cache: on cold start we prefetch the first 2k tokens for a few frequent prompts.
[01:23] Luca: that prefetch plus the 8-way batch, plus a request with a long output could push the working set above the driver allocation threshold. then the CUDA driver will throw an allocation error, sometimes the kernel hangs and the watchdog steps in.
[01:36] Nadia: are we talking about OOM that the OS kills, or the driver aborts the GPU?
[01:40] Luca: both flavors appear. in some traces dmesg shows "Out of memory: kill process" lines, which is the host OOM killer. in others we see the GPU watchdog timeout: "GPU hung" and "GPU reset" messages. the latter is typically a kernel launch timeout.
[01:53] Ethan: our nodes are G5-style 40GB cards, driver 535.x — we haven't upgraded recently.
[02:00] Priya: driver version is interesting — older drivers had some regression with pinned memory fragmentation. upgrading might help but we should reproduce first.
[02:08] Rosa: reproduction is tricky, it doesn't fail on dev clusters, only on prod under load.
[02:13] Luca: right, likely a combination of load pattern and fragmentation. couple of hypotheses: 1) KV cache prefetch is doing per-request allocations that are not recycled quickly, 2) batcher causes temporary combined peak working set, 3) repeated model swaps or quantization conversion code paths leaking host allocations.
[02:30] Ethan: is there known issue with cublasLt or one of the kernels that would cause a hang?
[02:34] Luca: there are known edge cases where certain kernel launches can block if memory is tight — particularly fused attention kernels or custom matmul kernels. we also have some runtime fallback where if a kernel fails we attempt a fallback to a slower kernel, but that fallback sometimes still triggers the watchdog if the device is under pressure.
[02:49] Rosa: what about retry semantics? when we see a runtime fail, do requests automatically retry? i saw some double-charges in our metrics, not sure if that's retries.
[02:57] Priya: good question — by default Redwood runtime will not silently retry non-idempotent calls, but for idempotent generation requests we have a retry policy that does single backoff and routes to a fallback model variant if available. retries will increase token counts and can inflate billing.
[03:16] Ethan: ah that explains it, we have a route set as idempotent for some of the batched calls... maybe that's causing thrash.
[03:23] Luca: can we check request ids for the failed windows? if retries happened they'd be visible in trace logs.
[03:28] Rosa: i'll pull the correlated request ids and screenshots.
[03:30] [03:30] (crosstalk)
[03:32] Luca: also, a quick triage step: collect nvprof / nvtrace during a failure window, record nvidia-smi every 5s, and collect dmesg and syslog. that will show if allocations spike and whether the GPU resets precede container restarts.
[03:46] Ethan: does Redwood provide a kv cache trace flag? i've seen --trace-kv mentioned in docs.
[03:49] Luca: yes, we recently added a --trace-kv runtime flag that logs cache hits/misses and prefetch activity with memory estimates. enabling that on one pod for a window should show if prefetch correlates with the OOMs.
[03:59] Rosa: ok we'll enable that on a canary service.
[04:02] Priya: what about node-level tuning? swap shenanigans?
[04:06] Luca: avoid swap on GPU nodes; swapping host memory can make latency unpredictable and can interact with pinned memory. also set Docker runtime to use --memory-swappiness=0 for the ML workload nodes. and ensure the kubelet eviction thresholds are tuned so pods are drained earlier rather than letting host OOM happen.
[04:20] Ethan: our kubelet eviction is default, so we might be hitting host OOM before pods are gracefully evicted.
[04:24] Nadia: is there an SDK-level workaround we can deploy quickly? like smaller batches or limit prefetch?
[04:31] Luca: yes, short-term mitigations: reduce batch size to 4, cap max_output_tokens per request, disable prefetch for the most volatile prompt set, and pin worker processes to GPUs with nvidia-smi topo settings where possible. medium-term: upgrade drivers, ensure pinned allocation reuse in runtime, and add a backpressure mechanism in the batcher.
[04:50] Rosa: backpressure — can Redwood runtime throttle incoming requests when memory pressure crosses a threshold?
[04:55] Luca: we have a soft OOM monitor in staging but not enabled in your cluster. we can provide an operator config that watches high-water memory and rejects or queues new requests, or shifts to a lighter model variant automatically. that's part of Redwood Optimize recommendations.
[05:07] Ethan: automatic model fallback sounds nice. what about latency impact? customers expect sub-200ms for some routes.
[05:13] Priya: fallbacks increase latency; we'd only do them for best-effort routes or when SLAs aren't strict. for strict p99 latency SLAs Dedicated capacity with headroom is recommended.
[05:22] Luca: another point — check for multi-tenancy noise: are other GPU jobs on the same node doing large cudaMallocs? nvidia-smi snapshots can reveal that. if the node is shared, fragmentation is worse. we recommend node isolation for critical routes.
[05:34] Rosa: our nodes are mixed, we do some batch offline ETL on same node overnight, could be the conflict.
[05:39] Nadia: that’s likely then. we wanted to save cost by mixing workloads but it's biting us.
[05:44] Priya: dedicated GPU pools for critical routes can reduce these noisy-neighbor issues; we can share pricing for Dedicated.
[05:49] Ethan: ok next, log formats: what traces do you need exactly?
[05:53] Luca: 1) runtime trace with --trace-kv enabled, 2) nvprof/nvtrace around the failure window, 3) continuous nvidia-smi top every 5s, 4) dmesg + journalctl for kernel messages, 5) pod YAMLs and node labels.
[06:05] Rosa: we'll collect and upload to the shared S3 link.
[06:07] Luca: one more subtle thing — quantization code paths: sometimes when we fall back from q4 to fp16 for a specific op we allocate a CPU-side temp buffer for upcasting, that can push host memory. check agent logs for "upcast temp alloc" messages.
[06:20] Ethan: i think we saw "alloc host mem" messages in the runtime logs.
[06:24] Luca: yep that's the one. it helps if the runtime caches those buffers and reuses them — we'll check the current release for a patch.
[06:32] Priya: any immediate red flags that would force a P0?
[06:35] Luca: not P0 yet; it's intermittent and has mitigations. if you see full node reboots or repeated watchdog resets causing customer-facing downtime, escalate. for now treat as P1: collect traces and enable mitigations.
[06:47] Rosa: what about the suggested kubelet eviction changes? specifically which thresholds?
[06:51] Luca: set memory.available to 100Mi for critical nodes? sorry that's too small — better: node allocatable reserves and kube-reserved to account for driver/pinning memory. ensure systemReserved and kubeReserved configured to subtract ~6-8GB on a 40GB card node to account for driver and pinned memory.
[07:09] Ethan: good, we'll prototype that on a canary node.
[07:13] Nadia: what about VPC and on-prem constraints? we run in a VPC with strict egress controls, will enabling profile tracing require opening ports?
[07:20] Priya: no, traces are collected locally and uploaded to your s3. we provide a small agentless script that tars logs and you can S3 put. no inbound connectivity needed.
[07:28] Rosa: are there any Redwood runtime flags we should flip immediately?
[07:31] Luca: disable automatic model hot-swap, cap batch size, enable --trace-kv, and set runtime env REDWOOD_KV_PREFETCH_LIMIT=2 as a temporary cap. also set REDWOOD_RUNTIME_RETRY=off to avoid hidden retries while debugging.
[07:45] Ethan: turning retries off is risky for some consumer routes — will that surface more failures to users?
[07:50] Priya: yes it will, but it's safer for debugging and avoids hidden double-billing and thrash. for a canary, it's ok.
[07:58] Rosa: ok we will do canary changes tonight.
[08:02] [08:02] (short pause)
[08:05] Luca: also capture the worker thread stack traces when you see a hung kernel — that helps us see which kernel is stuck. use gdb on the process core or send the perf samples.
[08:16] Ethan: noted.
[08:18] Priya: recap of next steps — Luca will produce a checklist of traces and flags; Rosa/Ethan will run canary changes and upload logs; Priya will share Dedicated pricing and security docs. follow-up repro session week of 11/17.
[08:34] Rosa: sounds good.
[08:36] Nadia: thanks everyone, appreciate it.
[08:38] Priya: thanks all, we'll sync soon.
